questions.question: What is the maximum throughput of USB 3.0 (USB 3.2 Gen 1)?
options: 5 Gbps (USB 3.2 Gen 1, blue port)
480 Mbps (legacy USB 2.0 High-Speed)
10 Gbps (USB 3.2 Gen 2, teal port)
40 Gbps (USB4 / Thunderbolt 4)
questions.explanation: USB 3.0 was rebranded USB 3.2 Gen 1 and operates at 5 Gbps. USB 2.0 = 480 Mbps. USB 3.2 Gen 2 doubled it to 10 Gbps. USB4 and Thunderbolt 4 reach 40 Gbps.

questions.question: Which component stores BIOS/UEFI settings while the PC is powered off?
options: The CPU L3 cache during sleep states
A reserved region on the boot SSD
CMOS RAM kept alive by a CR2032 coin cell
Standard system DRAM with refresh
questions.explanation: CMOS (Complementary Metal-Oxide Semiconductor) RAM holds the BIOS/UEFI settings and is powered by a small CR2032 coin-cell battery on the motherboard whenever main power is removed.

questions.question: A Windows PC shows 'Operating system not found' at power-on. Most likely cause?
options: Faulty stick of system RAM in slot 1
Wrong boot order or corrupted boot sector
GPU has failed and won't initialize
Network adapter driver crashed at boot
questions.explanation: The BIOS/UEFI cannot locate a bootable OS. Check boot order in firmware, confirm the SSD/HDD is detected, and run startup repair or 'bootrec /fixmbr' from Windows installation media.

questions.question: Which RAID level mirrors all data across exactly two disks for redundancy?
options: RAID 0 — striping for raw performance
RAID 5 — striping with distributed parity
RAID 10 — striped pairs of mirrors
RAID 1 — full mirror across two disks
questions.explanation: RAID 1 mirrors every block onto two drives. If one fails, the other has an identical copy. Usable capacity is 50%. Writes do not gain speed, but reads can be served from either disk.

questions.question: Which display interface carries digital video AND audio over a single cable?
options: S-Video — analog video, no audio
HDMI — digital video and audio
DVI-D — digital video, no audio
VGA — analog video, no audio
questions.explanation: HDMI carries both digital video and audio on one cable. VGA is analog video only. DVI-D is digital video only. DisplayPort also carries digital video plus audio.

questions.question: Which Windows utility scans the file system for errors and bad sectors?
options: Task Manager (taskmgr.exe)
Device Manager (devmgmt.msc)
CHKDSK (the chkdsk.exe utility)
Disk Defragmenter (dfrgui.exe)
questions.explanation: CHKDSK (Check Disk) verifies the file system and can flag bad sectors. 'chkdsk /f' fixes logical errors; 'chkdsk /r' implies /f and additionally locates bad sectors and recovers readable data.

questions.question: Why is thermal paste applied between a CPU and its heatsink?
options: Fills microscopic gaps for better heat transfer
Protects CPU pins from physical damage
Lubricates the fan bearings on the cooler
Improves electrical conductivity to the heatsink
questions.explanation: The IHS and the base of a cooler look flat but have microscopic pits. Thermal compound fills those gaps so heat conducts from the CPU into the heatsink instead of stagnating in air pockets.

questions.question: A laptop's wireless adapter shows as disabled in Device Manager. First step?
options: Flash the latest BIOS from the vendor site
Reinstall Windows to refresh all drivers
Check the Wi-Fi kill switch / Fn key, then BIOS
Replace the M.2 wireless card with a new one
questions.explanation: Many laptops have a physical Wi-Fi switch or an Fn key combo (e.g., Fn+F2) that disables wireless. Toggle it first. If still disabled, confirm Wi-Fi is enabled in firmware before assuming a driver or hardware fault.

questions.question: Which type of memory is used inside the CPU caches (L1/L2/L3)?
options: DDR4 SDRAM on the memory controller
DRAM — refreshed dynamic memory cells
NAND flash optimized for very low latency
SRAM — static memory, no refresh needed
questions.explanation: CPU caches use SRAM, which holds state in flip-flops with no refresh, so it is faster than the DRAM used for main system memory. SRAM is more expensive per bit and draws more power.

questions.question: Which Windows command displays the current IPv4 configuration?
options: tracert hostname
ipconfig /all
netstat -ano
questions.explanation: 'ipconfig' lists IP, subnet, and default gateway per adapter. 'ipconfig /all' also prints DHCP server, DNS servers, MAC address, and lease times — useful for DHCP and DNS troubleshooting.

questions.question: What does ESD stand for, and why does it matter when servicing PCs?
options: External Secure Drive — protected backup volume
Encrypted Storage Device — a self-encrypting disk
Electrostatic Discharge — can destroy chips silently
Extended System Diagnostics — a POST-level test
questions.explanation: Electrostatic discharge can carry thousands of volts that you cannot feel but that fry CPUs, RAM, and ICs. Use an anti-static strap bonded to chassis ground and work on an anti-static mat.

questions.question: A user reports 100% disk usage in Task Manager and a sluggish PC. Likely cause?
options: Background indexing/AV scan, or a failing HDD
Faulty monitor causing GPU contention
Defective RAM module producing read errors
Outdated video driver hooking disk I/O
questions.explanation: 100% disk usage often comes from Windows Search, antivirus scans, Windows Update servicing, or a dying mechanical drive. Inspect processes in Task Manager and run CHKDSK plus SMART checks on the drive.

questions.question: Key difference between 32-bit and 64-bit Windows installations?
options: 64-bit addresses far more RAM and runs 64-bit apps
64-bit is roughly twice as fast on identical hardware
32-bit is inherently more secure than 64-bit Windows
They are functionally identical for end users
questions.explanation: 32-bit Windows can only address roughly 4 GB of RAM. 64-bit Windows addresses vastly more and can run both 32-bit (via WOW64) and native 64-bit applications. Modern hardware ships with 64-bit Windows.

questions.question: Which built-in Windows tool manages programs that launch at sign-in?
options: Registry Editor (regedit.exe)
Task Manager → Startup tab (or msconfig)
Device Manager (devmgmt.msc tool)
Control Panel → Programs and Features
questions.explanation: Windows 10/11 exposes startup management in Task Manager's Startup tab. The legacy msconfig (System Configuration) tool also lists startup items and is handy when troubleshooting boot or sign-in delays.

questions.question: Primary purpose of a UPS (Uninterruptible Power Supply)?
options: Boost downlink internet bandwidth via QoS
Increase the efficiency of the PSU output
Cool rack-mounted servers via active airflow
Battery backup + surge protection for safe shutdown
questions.explanation: A UPS supplies battery power during outages and conditions incoming power. It gives connected workstations and servers time for an orderly shutdown and absorbs surges that would otherwise damage hardware.

questions.question: A PC emits three beeps at POST and fails to start. What does this usually mean?
options: RAM problem (per AMI/Award beep codes)
Drained CMOS coin-cell battery (CR2032)
Failing system hard drive or SSD module
CPU thermal protection kicked in early
questions.explanation: Beep codes vary by BIOS vendor, but three beeps on AMI/Award commonly indicate a RAM issue. Reseat the DIMMs, test one stick at a time, and try alternate slots to isolate the bad module or socket.

questions.question: Which file system does Windows install on the system drive by default?
options: FAT32 (4 GB file size cap)
exFAT (FAT successor, no journal)
NTFS (Windows-native, journaled)
ReFS (Storage Spaces / Server use)
questions.explanation: NTFS is the default for Windows installations. It supports large files and volumes, ACL permissions, EFS encryption, compression, and journaling. FAT32 is typically only used for small removable media.

questions.question: What is the function of BitLocker in Windows?
options: Manages Windows Update download bandwidth
Full-volume encryption tied to TPM keys
Cloud backup of user files to OneDrive
On-demand antimalware scanning service
questions.explanation: BitLocker encrypts entire volumes. If the drive is removed or the device stolen, data is unreadable without the BitLocker recovery key. Best practice is to pair BitLocker with a TPM 2.0 chip.

questions.question: What does POST do when a PC powers on?
options: Measures internet bandwidth from the firmware
Verifies network connectivity to the gateway
Self-tests CPU, RAM, and core devices pre-OS
Pushes a BIOS firmware update to the chipset
questions.explanation: Power-On Self-Test runs from BIOS/UEFI before the bootloader is loaded. It verifies CPU, memory, and core devices are present and functional, then hands off to the bootloader to start the OS.

questions.question: What does the NTFS permission 'Full Control' actually grant?
options: Read and write to existing files only
Read, write, modify, delete, take ownership
Execute existing binaries; no other access
Read-only access to files and folders
questions.explanation: Full Control on NTFS aggregates Read, Write, Execute, Modify, Delete, Change Permissions, and Take Ownership. It is the broadest standard NTFS permission and should be granted sparingly.

questions.question: What is the difference between an HDD and an SSD?
options: SSDs hold more data than HDDs of an identical size
Both technologies use the same underlying NAND flash
HDDs deliver faster sequential reads than SSDs do
HDD: spinning platters; SSD: NAND flash, no moving parts
questions.explanation: HDDs use rotating magnetic platters and a moving head (100–200 MB/s, shock-sensitive). SSDs use NAND flash with no moving parts — far faster (550 MB/s SATA, 3500+ MB/s NVMe), more durable, but pricier per GB.

questions.question: Which PCIe slot do modern discrete GPUs use for full bandwidth?
options: PCIe x16 slot (32 GB/s on PCIe 4.0)
PCIe x4 slot (NVMe or capture cards)
PCIe x8 slot (some workstation cards)
PCIe x1 slot (NIC or sound cards)
questions.explanation: PCIe x16 provides the bandwidth required by modern GPUs. PCIe 4.0 x16 = 32 GB/s bidirectional. x1 slots are for NICs and sound cards. Physical and electrical lane counts may differ, so check the manual.

questions.question: A PC powers on but the monitor stays blank. Which checks come first?
options: Update all drivers remotely via WSUS
Swap the CPU before any visual diagnostics
Reinstall Windows from recovery media
Monitor input, GPU/cable seat, POST beeps
questions.explanation: Start with the simplest causes: verify the monitor is powered and set to the right input, reseat the GPU and re-check the display cable, then listen for POST beep codes that point to RAM or GPU faults.

questions.question: Primary purpose of a TPM (Trusted Platform Module)?
options: Hardware key store + BitLocker + Secure Boot root
Acts as DRAM cache for the chipset memory
Controls USB port enumeration at boot time
Increases CPU base clock during boost states
questions.explanation: TPM 2.0 is a dedicated security chip. It stores cryptographic keys (including BitLocker), backs Secure Boot, supports measured boot, and is mandatory for Windows 11. Keys held in TPM cannot be extracted by removing the disk.

questions.question: What does a KVM switch let an operator do?
options: Manage hypervisor-hosted virtual machines
Run a Type-1 hypervisor on bare metal
Drive multiple PCs from one keyboard+mouse+monitor
Control VLANs on managed network switches
questions.explanation: A KVM (Keyboard/Video/Mouse) switch shares one console across multiple computers via a button or hotkey. It is common in server rooms and at technician benches managing several machines at once.

questions.question: Which Windows command repairs the Master Boot Record?
options: sfc /scannow (system file checker)
chkdsk /f (file system check)
diskpart clean (wipe a disk)
bootrec /fixmbr (repair MBR)
questions.explanation: From the Windows Recovery Environment: 'bootrec /fixmbr' rewrites the MBR, 'bootrec /fixboot' repairs the boot sector, and 'bootrec /rebuildbcd' rebuilds the Boot Configuration Data store.

questions.question: What is virtualization, and which CPU feature enables it efficiently?
options: Splitting a single drive into several primary partitions
Mounting a portion of system RAM as a fast disk drive
Dual-booting two operating systems natively on one PC
Running multiple guest OSes on one host via a hypervisor
questions.explanation: A hypervisor (ESXi, Hyper-V, KVM, VirtualBox) lets a single host run several guest OSes at the same time. Hardware acceleration via VT-x (Intel) or AMD-V — toggled in BIOS/UEFI — is required for good performance.

questions.question: What is the Windows Registry, and why does its health matter?
options: A read-only catalog of installed Microsoft Store apps
A flat list of currently mapped network drives only
Hierarchical key/value DB for OS + app settings
A signed manifest used during Windows Update
questions.explanation: The Registry is a hierarchical key/value database storing OS and application configuration. Key hives: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE (system-wide) and HKEY_CURRENT_USER (per-user). Corruption can prevent boot — always back up before editing.

questions.question: What is a System Restore point in Windows?
options: A full bare-metal image of the C: volume
A block-level snapshot of every user document
A shadow copy of every file in the user profile
A snapshot of system files, drivers, and registry
questions.explanation: System Restore captures a snapshot of system files, drivers, the registry, and selected app data. Rolling back returns Windows to that state without touching personal files. Triggered manually or before major changes.

questions.question: Which set matches the official Windows 11 minimum hardware requirements?
options: 1 GHz 64-bit CPU, 4 GB RAM, TPM 2.0, UEFI Secure Boot
Any Windows 10–capable PC, no additional checks needed
No hardware requirements; install runs on any 32-bit PC
32-bit CPU, 2 GB RAM, BIOS legacy, no TPM required
questions.explanation: Windows 11 requires a 1 GHz+ 64-bit CPU with 2+ cores, 4 GB RAM, 64 GB storage, UEFI firmware with Secure Boot, TPM 2.0, and a DirectX 12 GPU. The TPM 2.0 check is enforced by the installer.

questions.question: What does APIPA stand for, and which address range does it use?
options: Automatic Public IP Assignment — uses 1.x.x.x range
Automated Prefix IP Assignment — uses 10.x.x.x range
Advanced Private Internet Protocol — uses 172.x.x.x
Automatic Private IP Addressing — 169.254.0.0/16
questions.explanation: APIPA assigns a 169.254.x.x address when Windows cannot reach a DHCP server. Seeing 169.254.x.x means DHCP failed — check the cable, the DHCP scope, and reachability to the DHCP server.

questions.question: Which Windows tool manages disk partitions?
options: Device Manager — drivers, not partitions
Task Manager — processes, not partitions
Disk Management (diskmgmt.msc) or diskpart
CHKDSK — checks file system errors only
questions.explanation: Disk Management (diskmgmt.msc) creates, deletes, formats, and resizes partitions and assigns drive letters via a GUI. The diskpart CLI is the scriptable equivalent with more advanced options (used in recovery).

questions.question: What is the Windows pagefile (virtual memory)?
options: File on disk that extends RAM by paging out cold pages
A BIOS setting that toggles SLAT/EPT support
A reserved volume created by the BitLocker setup
A swap partition used only by Linux distributions
questions.explanation: pagefile.sys (typically C:\pagefile.sys) supplements physical RAM. When RAM is under pressure Windows pages cold memory to disk. A slow pagefile on an HDD makes the PC sluggish — moving it to SSD helps.

questions.question: Correct way to remove a USB drive safely in Windows?
options: Format the drive before unplugging it each time
Use 'Safely Remove Hardware' or Quick Removal policy
Run CHKDSK before unplugging the device
Yank the drive at any time; Windows handles it
questions.explanation: Removing a USB drive mid-write can corrupt data. 'Safely Remove Hardware' flushes pending writes. In Windows 10/11 the Quick Removal policy is the default, making it safe to unplug once write activity stops.

questions.question: Slow performance and frequent freezing on a mechanical HDD usually mean what?
options: Antivirus is misclassifying ordinary disk I/O as suspect
A failing memory module randomly stalling I/O requests
Imminent HDD failure — listen for clicks, check SMART
CPU thermal throttling kicking in and limiting cores
questions.explanation: Clicking, grinding, slow seeks, and freezes on an HDD point to mechanical decline. Check SMART (CrystalDiskInfo) — any 'Caution' or 'Bad' attribute means back up immediately and replace the drive.

questions.question: Primary purpose of Device Manager in Windows?
options: View, update, disable, and troubleshoot drivers
Manages user accounts and password policy
Controls Windows Update download settings
Manages startup applications at sign-in
questions.explanation: Device Manager (devmgmt.msc) lists hardware and driver state. A yellow exclamation = driver problem; a red X = disabled. Right-click to update, roll back, or uninstall. 'View → Show hidden devices' helps in tricky cases.

questions.question: What does it mean to 'image' a drive in IT support?
options: Take a bit-for-bit copy of an entire volume
Capture a screenshot of the desktop wallpaper
Defragment then compress the file system
Quick-format the drive prior to handing it off
questions.explanation: Drive imaging (Clonezilla, Macrium Reflect, Acronis) produces an exact bit-for-bit copy of a volume or disk. It is used for mass PC deployment, disaster recovery, and forensic preservation of evidence.

questions.question: Function of Microsoft Defender Antivirus in modern Windows?
options: A physical security alarm for office hardware
Built-in antivirus with real-time + cloud protection
A standalone network firewall replacement only
An on-device file backup and restore utility
questions.explanation: Microsoft Defender (formerly Windows Defender) is the built-in AV in Windows 10/11. It provides real-time protection, scheduled scans, cloud-delivered detections, and controlled folder access against ransomware.

questions.question: Difference between a clean install and an upgrade install of Windows?
options: Clean keeps user files; upgrade wipes them entirely on first boot
Clean: wipe + fresh install; upgrade: install over existing OS, keep apps
Upgrade install is preferred in every scenario over a clean install
Both produce an identical final system state in every measurable way
questions.explanation: Clean install: formats the drive and lays down a brand-new OS — best for resolving deep corruption. Upgrade install: lays new bits over the existing OS and preserves apps + settings — faster but can carry old issues forward.

questions.question: FIRST thing to check when a user says 'my PC won't turn on'?
options: Power cable, outlet, power strip, and front LED
Reinstall the operating system from scratch
Swap out the motherboard for a known-good board
Replace the PSU before any further diagnosis
questions.explanation: Always rule out the simple causes first: cable seated, wall outlet live, power strip on, UPS or surge protector functional, and the front-panel power LED responding when the button is pressed.

questions.question: Purpose of the Windows Event Viewer?
options: Manages programs that launch at sign-in
Controls installed hardware device drivers
Displays system, app, and security event logs
Monitors live LAN traffic on every NIC
questions.explanation: Event Viewer (eventvwr.msc) shows logs: System (hardware/driver), Application (program errors), and Security (logon/audit). Event IDs guide diagnosis — e.g., 4624 successful logon, 1000 application crash.

questions.question: What is the M.2 form factor for SSDs?
options: Slot on the motherboard for NVMe/SATA SSDs
A DDR4 memory module physical variant
External SATA SSD connector (eSATA)
A specific brand of consumer SATA SSD
questions.explanation: M.2 is a compact connector on the motherboard accepting NVMe (PCIe) or SATA SSDs. Common sizes: 2230/2242/2260/2280 (e.g., 2280 = 22 mm wide × 80 mm long). Confirm key (B, M, B+M) matches the slot.

questions.question: What does S.M.A.R.T. technology do for drives?
options: Manages RAID parity rebuilds at the controller
Self-Monitoring/Analysis/Reporting Technology
Encrypts data at rest with hardware AES keys
Speeds up HDD seek times via caching
questions.explanation: SMART monitors attributes like reallocated sectors, spin-up time, error rates, power-on hours, and temperature. Tools (CrystalDiskInfo) read SMART. Any 'Caution' or 'Fail' status means back up and replace the drive.

questions.question: What is Windows Sandbox?
options: A simple IP isolation rule in Defender Firewall
Cloud-based file backup that auto-versions data
Isolated, disposable desktop for untrusted apps
A persistent virtual hard disk for VM testing
questions.explanation: Windows Sandbox (Pro/Enterprise) is a lightweight, disposable VM using Hyper-V. Files, downloads, and installs inside it are discarded on close — ideal for safely opening suspicious attachments or installers.

questions.question: Cold boot vs warm boot — what's the difference?
options: Both refer to the temperature of the chassis
They are identical in software behavior
Cold = full power cycle; warm = OS-initiated restart
Cold boot skips POST and warm boot runs it
questions.explanation: Cold boot: full power-off and power-on — POST runs completely. Warm boot: software-initiated restart from the OS — clears RAM but some hardware state may not fully reset. Cold boots clear stuck hardware states.

questions.question: What is Windows Safe Mode used for?
options: A read-only backup capture of the registry
A network diagnostics-only WinPE environment
An admin-only user account elevation profile
Boot with minimal drivers/services for repair
questions.explanation: Safe Mode loads only essential drivers (basic display, keyboard, mouse). Safe Mode with Networking adds NIC drivers. Use it to remove drivers, run AV scans, fix boot, or undo system changes that prevent normal startup.

questions.question: Inkjet vs laser printer — key practical difference?
options: Laser printing is the better choice for any workload
Inkjet sprays liquid ink; laser fuses dry toner
Inkjet and laser use identical technology stacks
Inkjet technology is now considered obsolete by OEMs
questions.explanation: Inkjet sprays liquid ink onto paper — great for photos, slower, costly per page. Laser fuses toner with heat — fast, cheap per page at volume, sharp text. Receipt printers use thermal paper instead.

questions.question: Purpose of a POST diagnostic card?
options: A passive NIC tap used in packet capture
Hardware card displaying POST hex codes
A video capture card recording HDMI input
An external network tester for cable runs
questions.explanation: A POST card inserts into a motherboard slot (PCIe, PCI, or LPC) and shows POST hexadecimal codes as the system boots. It pinpoints where the boot process fails even when there is no display output yet.

questions.question: Difference between 32-bit and 64-bit applications on 64-bit Windows?
options: 64-bit apps are faster than 32-bit on the same CPU
32-bit apps will simply not run on 64-bit Windows
32-bit run under WOW64; 64-bit run native, more RAM
64-bit apps require special CPU silicon to launch
questions.explanation: 64-bit Windows runs 32-bit apps under the WOW64 layer (installed under Program Files (x86)), with a per-process 4 GB limit. Native 64-bit apps have no such cap. Drivers must match OS bitness exactly.

questions.question: MBR vs GPT partition tables — what's the practical difference?
options: MBR and GPT are functionally identical for end users
MBR supports an essentially unlimited partition count
MBR: legacy, 2 TB cap, 4 primary; GPT: UEFI, 128 parts
GPT is readable only by Linux operating systems today
questions.explanation: MBR is the legacy 512-byte partition scheme — 2 TB drive cap and 4 primary partitions. GPT uses GUIDs, supports up to 128 partitions, drives well over 2 TB, and is required for UEFI boot and Windows 11.

questions.question: Which Windows command verifies and repairs protected system files?
options: defrag c: /u
chkdsk c: /f
diskpart list
sfc /scannow
questions.explanation: 'sfc /scannow' (System File Checker) scans and repairs corrupted or missing protected system files. Run from an elevated prompt. If SFC cannot repair, run 'DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth' first.

questions.question: Purpose of UEFI Secure Boot?
options: Verifies signed bootloader before it can execute
Encrypts the system volume after the OS loads
Enables PXE network booting on every adapter
Speeds up the boot process by skipping POST
questions.explanation: Secure Boot checks digital signatures of UEFI drivers, EFI apps, and OS bootloaders against a trusted-key database (db). Unauthorized code is blocked at boot. Required for Windows 11; can be disabled for some Linux setups.

questions.question: Purpose of Windows Task Scheduler?
options: Schedules CPU thread priority for processes
Manages print queues across network printers
Automates tasks at times or on event triggers
Tracks user logon times for compliance audits
questions.explanation: Task Scheduler (taskschd.msc) runs commands or scripts based on triggers (time, logon, idle, event). Windows itself uses it for updates and maintenance; admins use it for backups, cleanups, and other automation.

questions.question: What is the difference between a virus and a worm?
options: Virus needs a host + user action; worm self-spreads
Viruses spread autonomously over flat networks
Worms are generally considered less dangerous
They mean exactly the same thing in practice
questions.explanation: A virus rides inside a host file and needs a user to execute it. A worm is standalone and self-propagates over networks by exploiting vulnerabilities — WannaCry (EternalBlue/SMB) spread without any user action.

questions.question: What does the Windows Print Spooler do, and what happens if it crashes?
options: The print head firmware inside the printer
The toner/ink delivery mechanism on the cartridge
A network-side LPR driver on the print server
Queues print jobs; crash = stuck jobs, restart service
questions.explanation: The Print Spooler service (spoolsv.exe) queues jobs and talks to printers. If it crashes, jobs pile up and nothing prints. Fix: restart 'Print Spooler' in services.msc — or 'net stop/start spooler' after clearing PRINTERS folder.

questions.question: Purpose of Windows Group Policy (GPO) in Active Directory?
options: Manages screen-saver settings on standalone PCs
Solely controls user password reset workflows
Manages only NTFS share permissions across a domain
Centrally pushes security/system settings to AD objects
questions.explanation: GPOs apply settings to AD users and computers — password policy, software deployment, drive maps, Firewall rules, BitLocker, USB restrictions, and hundreds of other knobs. Processed at startup and user logon.

questions.question: Modern ATX motherboards use which main power connector?
options: 20-pin
12-pin
24-pin
16-pin
questions.explanation: Modern ATX boards use a 24-pin main connector (it grew from 20-pin in older ATX). A separate 4 or 8-pin EPS12V connector supplies the CPU. High-end PSUs are usually modular for cleaner cable management.

questions.question: What is Microsoft Hyper-V?
options: A backup and image-restore tool for Windows
A remote desktop streaming protocol for thin clients
A Windows performance and telemetry optimizer
Microsoft's Type-1 hypervisor built into Windows Pro/Server
questions.explanation: Hyper-V is a Type-1 (bare-metal) hypervisor included with Windows Pro/Enterprise/Server. It needs CPU virtualization plus SLAT. WSL2 and Windows Sandbox build on Hyper-V infrastructure.

questions.question: Purpose of the Windows hosts file?
options: Manages every program that launches at sign-in
Local hostname→IP map at C:\Windows\...\drivers\etc
Defines Windows Defender Firewall inbound rules
Tracks installed device drivers for diagnostics
questions.explanation: The hosts file (C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts) overrides DNS for local name resolution. Format: '192.168.1.10 server1.local'. Malware sometimes edits it to redirect banking sites — review during incidents.

questions.question: What is a CAC (Common Access Card)?
options: An SDXC card variant used in cameras
DoD smart card with PKI certificates for auth
A specialized 10 Gb Ethernet network card
A removable solid-state storage device
questions.explanation: The CAC is a US Department of Defense smart card with embedded PKI certificates and cardholder data. It is used for physical entry and logical access (Windows logon, email signing/encryption, VPN). A smart-card reader is required.

questions.question: What is virtualization software, and which products are common examples?
options: A type of server-grade RAID controller card
A specialized Type 6 RAID parity scheme
Software hosting VMs: VMware, Hyper-V, VirtualBox
A cloud migration / lift-and-shift orchestrator
questions.explanation: Type 1 hypervisors (VMware ESXi, Hyper-V, Proxmox) run on bare metal. Type 2 (VMware Workstation, Oracle VirtualBox, Parallels) run as an app on a host OS. VT-x/AMD-V must be enabled in firmware for performance.

questions.question: Difference between virus, worm, and ransomware?
options: Worms typically require an email attachment to propagate
Ransomware is simply the newest kind of file-borne virus
All three are essentially the same category of malware
Virus: user-executed; Worm: self-spreads; Ransomware: encrypts
questions.explanation: Virus rides infected files (user runs it). Worm self-propagates over the network via vulnerabilities (WannaCry, Code Red). Ransomware encrypts data and demands payment — usually delivered via phishing or exposed RDP.

questions.question: Windows Event Viewer — which logs matter most for troubleshooting?
options: An on-the-wire packet capture (pcap) viewer
Application, System, Security; filter by Level
A startup-program manager replacement utility
A live CPU/RAM/disk performance graph viewer
questions.explanation: Event Viewer path: Windows Logs → Application/System/Security. For crashes, look 5–10 minutes before the symptom. For security, watch event 4625 (failed logon) and 4720/4726 (account changes).

questions.question: What is DNS, and what role does it play in everyday computing?
options: Encrypts HTTP traffic by negotiating TLS handshakes
Resolves hostnames to IPs via a hierarchical lookup
Hands out IP addresses to clients on the LAN
Determines routing of packets across the internet
questions.explanation: DNS turns names like www.example.com into IP addresses. Resolution order: browser cache → OS cache → hosts file → local resolver → ISP/public DNS → authoritative DNS. Troubleshoot with nslookup or dig.

questions.question: What is SSD wear leveling, and why does it matter?
options: The controller spreads writes across flash cells
A capacity-saving SSD compression algorithm
Active cooling for high-speed NVMe SSD modules
Deduplication of duplicate blocks across NAND
questions.explanation: NAND cells have a finite write endurance (e.g., 3 000–10 000 cycles for TLC). The SSD controller distributes writes so no single cell wears out early. Both dynamic and static wear-leveling are used.

questions.question: Docking station vs port replicator for laptops?
options: Port replicators typically include high-watt power delivery
The two terms are interchangeable in everyday usage
Dock = single-cable full desktop hookup; replicator = passthrough
A docking station is wireless and uses Wi-Fi 6E to connect
questions.explanation: Docking stations (USB-C / Thunderbolt) deliver displays, USB, Ethernet, audio, and up to 100 W power over one cable. Port replicators are simpler passthrough boxes that present roughly the same ports the laptop already has.

questions.question: Inkjet vs laser printers — what's the real difference?
options: Inkjet is the better fit for high-volume office workloads
Inkjet: liquid ink droplets; laser: dry toner + heat fuser
Both technologies are functionally identical for users
Laser printers cost noticeably less upfront than inkjets
questions.explanation: Inkjet sprays liquid ink — best for photos, lower upfront cost, higher cost per page. Laser fuses dry toner to paper with a heated roller — faster, sharper text, lower cost per page at scale.

questions.question: Which Windows command shows active TCP/UDP connections and listening ports?
options: tracert hostname (traces L3 route hop-by-hop)
ping hostname (sends ICMP echo to one IP)
netstat -an / netstat -b (connections + ports)
ipconfig /all (NIC, DHCP, and DNS details)
questions.explanation: 'netstat -an' lists all connections and listening ports by IP/port. 'netstat -b' adds the owning process (admin required). Unusual listeners (e.g., 4444) can point to malware. On Linux the equivalent is 'ss -tunap'.

questions.question: What is the Windows hosts file, and what is it used for?
options: Local hostname→IP overrides at drivers\etc\hosts
A read-only list of trusted internet certificates
The Security Account Manager (SAM) database file
The DHCP server scope configuration in services
questions.explanation: C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts maps hostnames to IPs locally and takes precedence over DNS. Used for dev (dev.local → 127.0.0.1) and ad-blocking; abused by malware to redirect domains.

questions.question: Should you defragment an SSD?
options: Both HDDs and SSDs benefit equally from defrag
Defrag of SSDs improves their service lifespan
Defrag HDDs, but NOT SSDs (TRIM handles SSDs)
SSDs need a defrag pass on a weekly schedule
questions.explanation: HDD heads physically seek, so consolidating files helps. SSDs have no seek penalty, and defragmenting them wastes write cycles. Windows auto-optimizes SSDs with TRIM and leaves traditional defrag to HDDs.

questions.question: Symptoms of failing RAM?
options: Printers refuse to print queued jobs reliably
Slow internet downloads from specific websites
Bluetooth peripherals fail to pair on first try
Random BSODs, app crashes, MemTest86 errors
questions.explanation: Failing RAM commonly causes random BSODs (especially MEMORY_MANAGEMENT or PAGE_FAULT_IN_NONPAGED_AREA), 'out of memory' app errors, and corruption. Confirm with MemTest86 for 2+ passes or Windows Memory Diagnostic.

questions.question: What does 802.11ax (Wi-Fi 6) improve over Wi-Fi 5?
options: OFDMA + MU-MIMO + TWT + 1024-QAM, dense efficiency
Wi-Fi 6 operates exclusively on the 2.4 GHz band
Wi-Fi 6 is meant only for outdoor mesh deployments
Wi-Fi 6 is a new wired Ethernet IEEE standard
questions.explanation: Wi-Fi 6 adds OFDMA (multi-client per channel), 8-stream MU-MIMO, Target Wake Time (saves IoT battery), 1024-QAM (higher throughput), and BSS coloring (less co-channel interference). Wi-Fi 6E adds the 6 GHz band.

questions.question: Difference between SATA, M.2 SATA, and M.2 NVMe SSDs?
options: All three deliver identical sequential throughput in real workloads
Any M.2 SSD shipped today defaults to using the NVMe protocol
NVMe SSDs all run on top of the legacy SATA AHCI protocol stack
SATA = 6 Gbps; M.2 SATA same; M.2 NVMe = PCIe, 3–7 GB/s
questions.explanation: M.2 is a form factor. M.2 SATA tops out at 6 Gbps (same as 2.5" SATA SSDs). M.2 NVMe uses PCIe directly — PCIe 3.0 ≈ 3.5 GB/s, PCIe 4.0 ≈ 7 GB/s. Check the M.2 slot type (SATA / NVMe / both) before buying.

questions.question: What is a CAB file in Windows?
options: Cabinet archive: drivers / updates / OS components
A compressed self-modifying virus payload format
A vendor-specific raw driver binary blob format
A motherboard UEFI/BIOS update image format
questions.explanation: CAB (Cabinet) is Microsoft's compressed archive format used for driver packages, Windows Update payloads (.cab and .msu), and OS component distribution. Use 'expand.exe' to extract; setup.exe often does this automatically.

questions.question: Effect of 'chkdsk /f /r' on a Windows volume?
options: Confirms LAN connectivity to the default gateway
Resets the cached DNS resolver entries on a NIC
Resets Windows Defender Firewall to defaults
/f fixes FS errors; /r adds bad-sector recovery
questions.explanation: 'chkdsk /f' fixes file-system errors. '/r' implies '/f' and additionally scans for bad sectors and tries to recover data from them. On the system volume it runs on reboot — never interrupt the scan mid-run.

questions.question: Difference between HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE and HKEY_CURRENT_USER?
options: HKLM: system-wide config; HKCU: per-user profile
HKCU stores all device driver hardware settings
HKLM is permanently mounted as read-only
Both hives store completely identical content
questions.explanation: HKLM (HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE) holds machine-wide settings — SOFTWARE, SYSTEM, SAM, SECURITY — admin required to modify. HKCU (HKEY_CURRENT_USER) holds the logged-on user's settings and is loaded from HKEY_USERS\<SID>.

questions.question: What does 'jailbreaking' (iOS) or 'rooting' (Android) do?
options: Repairs a physically damaged mobile device
Backs up phone data to the iCloud or Google account
Removes vendor/carrier restrictions to gain root
Performs a factory reset on the mobile device
questions.explanation: Jailbreak/root bypasses manufacturer + carrier locks to grant elevated privileges. Risks: app-store sandbox removed, no OTA updates, malware can access the entire OS, and warranty/MDM compliance broken.

questions.question: What does MDM (Mobile Device Management) let admins control?
options: A fully featured mobile operating system kernel itself
PIN policy, app push, remote wipe, work/personal split
A pure backup-and-restore service for mobile device data
An on-site mobile device screen and battery repair shop
questions.explanation: MDM (Intune, Jamf, Workspace ONE) enrolls devices, enforces compliance (encryption, PIN length), pushes/blocks apps, allows remote lock/wipe, supports geofencing, and gates email via conditional access.

questions.question: What is the Windows Boot Configuration Data (BCD) store?
options: A signed Windows service description manifest
Modern boot store replacing boot.ini (bcdedit/bootrec)
A separate database of installed hardware drivers
A vendor-specific BIOS update payload archive
questions.explanation: BCD replaced boot.ini starting with Windows Vista. It lives in the EFI System Partition (UEFI) or on the System Reserved partition (BIOS). Edit with bcdedit.exe; rebuild with 'bootrec /rebuildbcd' from WinRE.

questions.question: Why use a ticket-based IT support system?
options: A general-purpose user time-tracking utility only
Issuing physical badges for company-wide events
Tracks requests with SLA, history, escalation, KB
A billing platform unrelated to support workflow
questions.explanation: Help-desk ticketing (ServiceNow, Jira Service Management, Freshservice, Zendesk) gives each request a unique ID, an assignee, and an SLA timer. It produces accountability, trend analysis, and a searchable knowledge base.

questions.question: What is the Windows Task Manager, and what are its key tabs?
options: Generic system backup and snapshot utility
On-board hardware diagnostic POST-card display
Processes, Performance, Startup, Services tabs
Software installer (replaces winget/Add-Remove)
questions.explanation: Task Manager tabs: Processes (running apps + background tasks), Performance (CPU/RAM/Disk/Network), Startup (manage sign-in autostart — key for slow boot), Services, Users, Details. Open with Ctrl+Shift+Esc.

questions.question: What is a driver rollback, and when would you use it?
options: Removes every driver from the running OS image
Updates every device driver automatically at boot
Reverts to the previous driver after a bad update
Performs a clean reinstall of Windows itself
questions.explanation: Driver rollback (Device Manager → Properties → Driver tab → Roll Back Driver) is the fastest fix when a driver update breaks a device. Available only if the previous version is still cached by Windows.

questions.question: What do the SFC and DISM commands do?
options: SFC verifies system files; DISM repairs the image store
Standalone antivirus and antimalware scanning tools
Disk partition formatting and quick-erase utilities
Network connectivity and DNS diagnostics commands
questions.explanation: Sequence for OS file corruption: 'DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth' (repairs the WinSxS component store) → 'sfc /scannow' (replaces protected files using the repaired store). Both require an elevated prompt.

questions.question: Older CCFL LCD laptops have an inverter board. What does it do?
options: Stops the screen flickering on AC adapter loss
Replaces a damaged LCD ribbon cable connector
Decodes HDMI/DisplayPort audio signal from the GPU
Converts DC to high-voltage AC for the CCFL backlight
questions.explanation: On CCFL-backlit laptops the inverter steps 12 V DC up to high-voltage AC needed by the fluorescent tube. Symptoms of inverter failure: very dim screen with image faintly visible. Modern LED backlights don't need an inverter.

questions.question: BIOS vs UEFI — what is the practical difference?
options: UEFI is fundamentally less secure than legacy BIOS
BIOS and UEFI are interchangeable terms today
Legacy BIOS boots a system noticeably faster than UEFI
BIOS = legacy 16-bit/MBR; UEFI = modern, GPT, Secure Boot
questions.explanation: UEFI advantages over legacy BIOS: Secure Boot (signed bootloader), GPT support for >2 TB drives and 128 partitions, faster pre-OS init, mouse-driven setup, network boot (PXE). Required for Windows 11.

questions.question: What does UEFI Secure Boot defend against?
options: Whole-disk data theft on a powered-off drive
Requires a TPM chip to be physically present
Unsigned/malicious bootloaders, bootkits, rootkits
An attacker setting a BIOS supervisor password
questions.explanation: Secure Boot validates the signature of every UEFI driver, EFI application, and OS bootloader against a trusted-key database (db) before execution. It blocks bootkits/rootkits and is required for Windows 11.

questions.question: Practical difference between 32-bit and 64-bit Windows versions?
options: 32-bit is consistently more stable than 64-bit
64-bit is just a marketing relabel of 32-bit
Only raw CPU speed differs between the two
64-bit: addresses >4 GB RAM and runs 64-bit apps
questions.explanation: 32-bit Windows tops out at ≈4 GB usable RAM. 64-bit Windows addresses far more (current CPUs ~1 TB practical), runs both 32-bit (WOW64) and 64-bit apps, and is now the only edition shipping with Windows 11.

questions.question: ipconfig /release vs ipconfig /renew — what do they do?
options: Reset Windows Defender Firewall to its defaults
/release drops the DHCP lease; /renew requests new IP
Clear the local DNS resolver cache on every adapter
Reload the network adapter driver in the OS kernel
questions.explanation: 'ipconfig /release' drops the DHCP lease; 'ipconfig /renew' requests a fresh address. Use both when a device has the wrong IP, a duplicate IP, or APIPA (169.254.x.x). 'ipconfig /flushdns' clears stale DNS entries.

questions.question: A UPS (Uninterruptible Power Supply) protects against what, and what topologies exist?
options: A generic server power management software stack tool
Battery backup + surge: Standby / Line-Int / Online
Another brand name for a high-watt modular ATX PSU
A rack-mounted power distribution unit (PDU) device
questions.explanation: UPS provides battery and surge protection. Topologies: Standby (cheap, brief gap on switchover), Line-Interactive (handles minor voltage swings without battery), Online/Double-Conversion (cleanest power, always on battery).

questions.question: Which Windows tools display logs of OS, app, and security events?
options: Performance Monitor and Resource Monitor only
Reliability Monitor (perfmon /rel) — single source
Event Viewer (eventvwr.msc) — multiple log channels
Task Manager → App History tab (24-hour view)
questions.explanation: Event Viewer is the primary log viewer. Channels: System (drivers/hardware), Application (program errors), Security (logon/audit). Use filter-by-level and event ID lookups (e.g., 4624 logon success) to scope incidents.

questions.question: What is dual-channel RAM, and how must it be installed?
options: Any pair of DIMMs in any slots gives dual-channel mode
Dual-channel typically requires four identical sticks
Matched pair in paired slots (A2+B2) per the manual
Any RAM combination works fine for dual-channel mode
questions.explanation: Dual-channel doubles memory bandwidth by accessing two DIMMs in parallel. The motherboard manual specifies which slots pair (typically A2+B2 first). Mismatched size or speed often falls back to single-channel.

questions.question: Why is thermal compound important on a CPU?
options: A cleaning agent applied before reseating coolers
Holds the heatsink mechanically in place over the CPU
Fills micro-gaps; dried paste = CPU overheating
A type of liquid-cooling working fluid in the loop
questions.explanation: Air is a poor thermal conductor. Thermal paste fills microscopic pits between the CPU IHS and the heatsink so heat flows efficiently. Old or pumped-out paste is a common cause of CPU thermal throttling and shutdown.

questions.question: What is Windows Safe Mode useful for?
options: A password-protected admin sign-in screen mode
An administrator-only Windows feature lockout view
Boot with minimal drivers/services — repair shape
A factory-reset profile that wipes the system drive
questions.explanation: Safe Mode loads only essential drivers — no third-party. Use it to undo bad driver/software installs, scan for malware that runs at startup, or recover from BSOD-on-boot. Access via Shift+Restart → Advanced Options.

questions.question: What is a Blue Screen of Death (BSOD), and what does it tell you?
options: Indicates a full Windows reinstall is required to recover
A virus infection indicator and nothing else by design
Caused exclusively by hardware faults, not driver faults
Kernel crash with stop code; check minidump + Event log
questions.explanation: A BSOD is a kernel-level fault. The stop code (IRQL_NOT_LESS_OR_EQUAL, MEMORY_MANAGEMENT, etc.) plus minidumps in C:\Windows\Minidump and Event Viewer System log identify the root cause — bad driver, RAM, or disk.

questions.question: What is the MBR vs GPT difference for disk partitioning?
options: The two schemes are completely identical in practice
GPT is less reliable than MBR for data integrity
MBR: 2 TB cap, 4 primary; GPT: 9.4 ZB, 128, UEFI
MBR supports much larger drives than GPT does
questions.explanation: MBR is the legacy 1983-era scheme: 2 TB drive cap, 4 primary partitions (Extended/Logical worked around it), 32-bit LBA. GPT (UEFI) uses GUIDs, supports up to 128 partitions and drives well past 2 TB, with a redundant table.

questions.question: What is the function of the PSU, and how do you size one?
options: Stores AC power for emergency outages on the wall side
Conditions signal quality on internal motherboard cables
Dynamically regulates the CPU base clock and boost states
Converts AC→DC rails (3.3/5/12 V); size: TDP × 1.2–1.5
questions.explanation: The PSU converts AC mains to DC rails: 12 V (CPU, GPU, motors), 5 V (drives, USB), 3.3 V (RAM, logic). Add up component TDPs (CPU + GPU dominate) and add 20–50% headroom. Prefer 80+ Bronze/Gold certified units.

questions.question: Differences between NTFS, FAT32, and exFAT?
options: FAT32 natively supports files larger than 4 GB on any OS
NTFS: ACLs+journal; FAT32: universal but 4 GB cap; exFAT: large files
All three file systems behave identically in everyday Windows use
NTFS is cross-platform read/write by default on macOS and Linux
questions.explanation: NTFS: best for Windows volumes — security, journaling, no practical file size cap. FAT32: universal compatibility but 4 GB per file. exFAT: FAT32's successor with large-file support and broad compatibility — good for USB/SD media.

questions.question: What are typical ESD (Electrostatic Discharge) precautions when servicing?
options: Prevents data loss only during repairs in progress
A formal safety requirement only for PSU work
A guard against electric shock to the technician
Anti-static strap to ground, anti-static mat, ESD bag
questions.explanation: ESD can reach thousands of volts — invisible to humans but fatal to ICs. Mitigations: wrist strap bonded to earth ground, anti-static mat, ESD bags for components, touch the bare chassis before handling, avoid carpet.

questions.question: POST (Power-On Self-Test) — what does it do?
options: A scheduled shutdown self-diagnostic at midnight
A user-initiated memory test launched from Windows
Firmware self-test of CPU/RAM/GPU/storage pre-OS
A BIOS firmware update push from the OEM cloud
questions.explanation: POST runs every boot from BIOS/UEFI: it tests CPU, basic RAM, discovers storage/GPU, and checks keyboard before handing off. Failures are signaled via beep codes (1=OK, continuous=RAM, etc.) or UEFI on-screen codes.

questions.question: What does a 'no boot device found' error usually point to?
options: The power supply has failed completely
Boot order wrong, corrupt MBR/BCD/EFI, dead disk
The GPU has failed mid-POST sequence
A failed memory module preventing kernel load
questions.explanation: 'No boot device' means the firmware can't find a bootable disk. Steps: (1) enter BIOS, confirm the drive is detected; (2) check boot order; (3) if detected, boot from USB and run 'bootrec /fixmbr' or 'bootrec /rebuildbcd'.

questions.question: A Windows 11 Pro laptop must be added to an Active Directory domain. Which TWO are required?
options: Credentials authorized to join computers to the domain
Network reach to a domain controller and DNS server
A static public IPv4 address allocated to the laptop
BitLocker encryption enabled on the system volume first
questions.explanation: Domain join needs DC reachability over the network (DNS resolves SRV records, then LDAP/Kerberos) and credentials authorized to create or reuse a computer account. Public IPs and BitLocker are not domain-join prerequisites.
